answer.rationale: The threat is specifically price-driven and concentrated in price-sensitive SMB accounts, so the levers with the strongest verified evidence (memory_86/exp_86 shortened onboarding, memory_91 activation messaging) do not actually address the churn conversations happening this week; they improve time-to-value for new accounts, not the price objection of existing ones. Promotional pricing is the only candidate aimed at the actual mechanism, so it is the right direction — but it should not be rolled out broadly today. Two reasons. First, memory_73 is an unverified consolidated summary; the two summaries I was able to trace back to source this cycle both proved lossy in the same direction. memory_31 read as a clean win, but exp_31 shows 30-day retention -1% and a result that did not replicate outside SMB — the negative and the scope limit were both dropped in consolidation. That is direct evidence that these summaries compress toward optimism, so memory_73's 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' should be read as an upper bound with unknown retention, margin, and segment-scope caveats stripped out. Second, pricing is the least reversible lever on the list: discounting under a competitor's cut sets an anchor, trains the base to expect concessions, selects for the most price-elastic (and least durable) accounts, and can invite a further cut from the competitor. Acquisition and revenue lift measured in a calm period says little about a discount issued mid-price-war, so even a faithful memory_73 would be off-distribution here. A small guarded test — bounded segment, explicit expiry, held-out control, and instrumentation on margin and post-discount retention, not just signup and revenue — buys the information memory_73 never recorded at a cost the company can absorb, and keeps the broad-rollout option open for next week when the archive reopens and memory_73 can be traced to source. Against the stated objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, a guarded test dominates a broad discount whose durable-revenue effect is genuinely unknown. Urgency from leadership raises the cost of delay, not the reliability of the evidence.
